content.text:
**LLM inference engineering** for production serving focuses on maximizing GPU utilization, throughput, and latency while handling dynamic, concurrent workloads efficiently. Key challenges include high memory demands from the KV cache (which grows with sequence length), the compute-bound prefill phase versus memory-bandwidth-bound decode phase, variable request lengths, and the need for stable performance under load.[[1]](https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/vllm-sglang-trtllm-comparison)[[2]](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-inference-optimization/)

Modern systems address these through architectural innovations in scheduling, memory management, and hardware-specific optimizations.

### Core Optimization Techniques
These techniques are foundational and often combined in production frameworks:

- **KV Cache + PagedAttention**: Standard autoregressive decoding recomputes attention over all prior tokens, but the KV cache stores precomputed keys/values to avoid this. Naive contiguous allocation leads to fragmentation and waste (often 60-80% of memory). **PagedAttention** (pioneered in vLLM) treats the KV cache like OS virtual memory—splitting it into fixed-size blocks allocated on demand and managed via a block table. This reduces waste dramatically (to ~4%), enables larger effective batch sizes, and supports longer contexts or more concurrent requests (2-4x throughput gains).[[1]](https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/vllm-sglang-trtllm-comparison)[[3]](https://zylos.ai/research/2026-01-15-llm-inference-optimization/)

- **Continuous (or In-Flight) Batching**: Traditional static batching waits for all requests in a batch to complete, leaving the GPU idle as shorter requests finish. Continuous batching adds new requests dynamically as slots free up (iteration-level scheduling). This keeps the GPU busy, improving throughput significantly (up to 23x in some cases) while reducing latency variance.[[1]](https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/vllm-sglang-trtllm-comparison)[[4]](https://mbrenndoerfer.com/writing/continuous-batching)

- **Chunked Prefill**: Long prompts can dominate a batch and stall shorter decode-heavy requests. Chunking splits prefill across iterations, improving scheduler fairness and overall system responsiveness.[[1]](https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/vllm-sglang-trtllm-comparison)

- **Quantization**: Reduces precision (e.g., FP16 → FP8/INT8 or lower) to cut memory footprint and boost compute throughput on Tensor Cores. Common methods include GPTQ, AWQ, and weight-only quantization. FP8 often delivers 30%+ speedups with minimal quality loss.[[3]](https://zylos.ai/research/2026-01-15-llm-inference-optimization/)

- **Speculative Decoding**: A smaller "draft" model proposes multiple tokens; the larger target model verifies them in parallel. Accepted tokens are kept; rejected ones trigger standard decoding. This can yield 2-3x speedups with no quality degradation via rejection sampling.[[5]](https://www.morphllm.com/llm-inference-optimization)

- **Prefix/Radix Caching**: Many workloads share prompt prefixes (e.g., system prompts, RAG templates). Radix-tree or prefix caching reuses computed KV states, avoiding redundant prefill work.[[1]](https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/vllm-sglang-trtllm-comparison)

- **Kernel and Execution Optimizations**: FlashAttention (and variants like FlashInfer), CUDA graphs (for low-overhead decode), kernel fusion, and Tensor Core utilization maximize hardware efficiency.[[6]](https://northflank.com/blog/vllm-vs-tensorrt-llm-and-how-to-run-them)

Additional production levers include tensor/pipeline/expert parallelism for multi-GPU scaling, model-specific compilation, and smart request routing.

### Key Frameworks for Production Serving
- **vLLM**: Widely adopted open-source engine emphasizing ease of use and efficiency. Core strengths: PagedAttention, continuous batching, prefix caching, chunked prefill, quantization, CUDA graphs, and broad hardware support (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, TPUs). Excellent for general workloads with an OpenAI-compatible API. Often the best balance for dynamic, long-context, or MoE models.[[1]](https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/vllm-sglang-trtllm-comparison)[[7]](https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2025/10/30/why-vllm-best-choice-ai-inference-today)

- **TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA)**: Engine-centric approach with deep NVIDIA GPU optimizations (custom kernels, CUDA graphs, in-flight batching, advanced quantization like FP8). Requires model conversion/compilation into a TensorRT engine for peak performance but delivers the highest throughput/latency on H100s and similar hardware. Best for NVIDIA-centric, latency-sensitive production deployments; higher setup complexity.[[8]](https://docs.rafay.co/blog/2025/04/28/choosing-your-engine-for-llm-inference-the-ultimate-vllm-vs-tensorrt-llm-guide/)[[6]](https://northflank.com/blog/vllm-vs-tensorrt-llm-and-how-to-run-them)

- **SGLang**: Strong on runtime optimizations like RadixAttention for prefix reuse, continuous batching, and structured generation. Competitive with vLLM, especially for workloads with high prefix overlap.[[1]](https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/vllm-sglang-trtllm-comparison)

- **Others**: Hugging Face Text Generation Inference (TGI) for ecosystem integration; NVIDIA NIM for managed, optimized containers combining the above; specialized solutions for specific hardware.

Benchmarks (e.g., on H100s with ShareGPT or long-context datasets) show trade-offs: vLLM often excels in TTFT + throughput balance for mixed workloads, while TensorRT-LLM can lead in raw NVIDIA performance when tuned.[[1]](https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/vllm-sglang-trtllm-comparison)

### Production Best Practices
- **Metrics to optimize**: TTFT (time-to-first-token), TPOT/ITL (time-per-output-token/inter-token latency), end-to-end latency, throughput (tokens/sec or requests/sec), and GPU utilization/memory efficiency. Balance latency vs. throughput based on use case (e.g., chat vs. batch processing).
- **Deployment**: Use OpenAI-compatible servers; enable features like `--enable-prefix-caching`, `--enable-chunked-prefill`, and appropriate quantization. Monitor KV cache usage and tune `--gpu-memory-utilization`.
- **Scaling**: Combine with distributed inference (tensor/pipeline parallelism) and autoscaling. Consider hardware independence vs. peak performance.
- **Trade-offs**: NVIDIA-specific engines offer max perf but risk lock-in; general frameworks like vLLM prioritize flexibility and ease. Quantization and speculative decoding add complexity but compound gains.
- **Ecosystem**: Integrate with orchestration (Kubernetes), monitoring, and cost tracking. Test end-to-end with realistic traffic (variable lengths, concurrency).

For hands-on work, start with vLLM docs or NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM tutorials. Recent comparisons (2025-2026) highlight that no single framework wins universally—evaluate on your models, workloads, and hardware.[[1]](https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/vllm-sglang-trtllm-comparison)

This field evolves rapidly with new kernels, attention variants (e.g., FlashAttention-3), and frameworks, so benchmark regularly.
